summary: This unit teaches you to straighten hair with chemical relaxers safely: how hydroxide and thio products work, how to consult, check the scalp and test, how to protect the client, how to apply a virgin relaxer and a retouch, how to rinse, neutralise and condition, and what to do when something goes wrong. You will also learn about texturisers, natural and transitioning hair, aftercare, and the safe storage and disposal of relaxers.

blocks.p: A chemical relaxer permanently straightens or loosens curly and coily hair. It is one of the most profitable services in a Jamaican salon and one of the most dangerous. Done well, it gives smooth, manageable hair that stays straight until it is cut off. Done badly, it burns the scalp, burns the eyes, and breaks the hair. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it demands the most care of any unit you have met.

Everything in this unit comes back to four rules: **test first, protect the client and yourself, time from the first application, and rinse at once if the client feels burning.** Follow the maker's instructions every time, because products differ.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon on training heads: a relaxer retouch on new growth, and a virgin relaxer or texturiser on natural hair. The assessor watches your consultation, tests, protection, order of application, timing, rinsing and safety as well as the result.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: On a real client, never go ahead if the scalp is broken, if tests are positive, or if the hair has a history that does not suit the product. Rebooking is always better than a burn.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The cortex is held in shape by three kinds of bond. Curly hair has many disulphide bonds arranged unevenly. A relaxer breaks them so that the hair can be smoothed straight.

head: Bond
Strength
Changed by
rows: Hydrogen bonds
Weak, many
Water and heat (temporary)
Salt bonds
Weak
Acids and alkalis (temporary)
Disulphide bonds
Strong, fewer
Relaxers and perms (permanent)

head: Type
Active ingredient
How it works
Notes
rows: Lye (sodium hydroxide)
Sodium hydroxide.
Very alkaline (high pH). It swells the hair and breaks disulphide bonds, and changes them into new, permanent bonds (lanthionine). This is **lanthionisation**.
Fast and strong; gives very straight hair; more risk to the scalp. Usually a 'base' relaxer: a protective cream is put on the scalp.
No-lye (guanidine hydroxide)
Guanidine hydroxide, made when a cream (calcium hydroxide) is mixed with an activator (a liquid containing guanidine carbonate).
Same result: lanthionisation. Mixed **just before use**.
Often 'no-base': base cream is still put on the hairline and ears. Can leave calcium build-up that dulls the hair; some clients' hair becomes dry.
Thio (ammonium thioglycolate)
Ammonium thioglycolate, a reducing agent.
Breaks disulphide bonds by adding hydrogen (reduction). The bonds are rebuilt in the straight shape by an **oxidising neutraliser** (usually hydrogen peroxide or sodium bromate).
Also used in perms. Different chemistry from hydroxide.
Texturiser
A relaxer (usually hydroxide) left on for a shorter time.
Loosens the curl but does not straighten it.
For clients who want looser curls, not straight hair.

ul: A hydroxide relaxer is **very alkaline** (high pH, around 12 to 14). That is why it works and why it burns skin and eyes.
Normal hair and skin are slightly acid (about pH 4.5 to 5.5); neutral is pH 7.
Relaxing changes the hair **permanently**. Only new growth is natural.

A hydroxide relaxer and a thio product must **never** be used on the same head, one over the other. They are not compatible and the mixture can cause severe breakage. Always ask which was used before.

head: Strength
For
Comment
rows: Mild (gentle)
Fine, porous, colour-treated or fragile hair; sensitive scalps
If the maker allows it at all on treated hair.
Regular (normal)
Medium texture, healthy hair
The usual choice.
Super (strong)
Coarse, resistant hair
Only if the hair needs it; more risk.

blocks.p: The right strength comes from the **hair analysis, the strand test and the maker's instructions**, not from habit or what you used on the last client. Coarse hair usually needs the strongest relaxer the maker allows; fine hair needs the mildest.

head: Ask about
Why
rows: Past relaxers: product type (hydroxide or thio), strength, date, who applied it, any problems
To choose the right product and know where the line of demarcation is.
Colour, bleach, henna, home dyes, keratin and smoothing treatments
Some react badly with relaxer or weaken the hair. Metallic salts and compound henna can react.
Home products, including 'natural' relaxers and kits
Unknown products may be incompatible.
Previous reactions: burns, scalp soreness, allergies
To plan protection or rule the service out.
Health: pregnancy, illness, medicines
May affect the hair and scalp; follow the Centre's rules and the maker's instructions.
What she wants: straight, looser curl, how long it must last
To agree the service and the product.

ul: Look for **cuts, scratches, scabs (abrasions), sores, redness and infection**.
The client must **not scratch her scalp** or have it brushed hard for a few days before a relaxer: broken skin lets the chemical burn.
If you find abrasions, **do not relax today**: rebook when the scalp has healed.
If there is any sign of infection, no service; refer kindly and privately.

head: Check
What it tells you
rows: Porosity
Porous hair takes the relaxer fast and can over-process.
Elasticity
Poor elasticity (snaps, or stretches and stays) means do not relax now: give conditioning and protein treatments first.
Texture
Fine, medium or coarse: guides the strength.
Density
More hair means more sections and time to apply.
New growth
Measure it; on a retouch, you apply only to this.
Condition
Damage, breakage, previous overlap, line of demarcation.

head: Test
How
What it shows
rows: Skin test
As the maker says, on the skin, left for the maker's time.
Allergy to the product.
Strand test
Apply the relaxer to a few strands (a small hidden section), time it and check.
How the hair reacts and roughly how long it needs; whether it can take the relaxer.
Porosity and elasticity tests
As in the consultation.
Hair strength and how fast it will process.
Incompatibility test
Cut hairs in a peroxide and ammonia mixture (or the maker's test); look for bubbling, heat or discolouring.
Metallic salts or other products that react with the relaxer.

head: Finding
What to do
rows: Abrasions or sores on the scalp
Do not relax today; rebook when healed.
Poor elasticity; breakage
No relaxer now: give conditioning treatments, trim, retest.
Positive skin test
No relaxer with that product.
Thio history on the hair
Never put a hydroxide relaxer over it.
Metallic salts or compound henna
No relaxer on that hair: it can react and damage the hair.
Recent colour or lightening, hair weak
Strand test; mild strength if the maker allows it at all; otherwise postpone.
Client unwilling or unsure
Do not push; offer other options.

blocks.note: Ask the client to agree to the service after you have explained what a relaxer does, the risks and the aftercare. This is **informed consent**. Record it on the card.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Read the **maker's instructions and the safety data sheet**. Know where the eyewash or clean running water is, and where the first aid kit and accident book are.
Check the area is **well ventilated**, so fumes do not irritate eyes or breathing.

Have everything ready before you start: relaxer (mixed just before use if it needs an activator), plastic bowl, brush or applicator, tail comb, clips, base cream, neutralising shampoo, conditioner, a timer, towels, cotton wool.
Do not use metal bowls or tools with relaxer.

head: Item
Why
rows: Chemical-resistant gloves
Relaxer burns the skin. Use gloves as the maker says.
Protective apron or gown
Protects your clothes and skin.
Client: chemical cape, towel, neck strip
Protects her clothes, neck and shoulders.
Eye protection if the Centre requires it
Splashes to the eyes are serious.

flow: Check the scalp again for abrasions
Do not shampoo the hair before a hydroxide relaxer: the scalp's natural oil helps protect it from the chemical (follow the maker)
Gown the client; protect her neck and clothes
Section the dry hair into four with a tail comb and clips
Apply base cream as the product needs
On a retouch, protect the previously relaxed hair as the maker says
Have the timer ready

head: Relaxer
Where base cream goes
rows: Base relaxer (usually lye)
Over the whole scalp, the hairline and the ears: a thick layer of petroleum-based base cream protects the skin.
No-base relaxer
On the hairline, the ears and the nape, and around any sensitive area. The scalp is not coated, because the product is milder and needs the scalp's natural oil.

ul: Base cream must **not** get on the hair you are about to relax: it blocks the relaxer.
Protect the **edges** and the nape: the hair is fine and processes faster.
Check the client is comfortable and has nothing on her lap that can be spoiled.

blocks.note: Do not scratch, rub or brush the scalp before the service. Comb gently with a wide-tooth comb. A scratch you cannot see can burn badly.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Applying a relaxer: virgin and retouch

blocks.p: A **virgin** relaxer goes onto hair that has never been chemically straightened. The hair near the scalp processes faster than the ends because of body heat, and the hair at the back is often more resistant than the front and edges. So the order of application matters.

flow: Gloves on; four sections; timer ready
Start at the most resistant area, usually the back
Take thin partings and apply the relaxer to the mid-lengths and ends first, keeping a short distance (about 1 cm, or as the maker says) from the scalp
Move to the other sections in order; keep the product off the scalp
Start the timer at the first application
Go back and apply to the roots and scalp area
Apply last to the hairline and edges, which are finer and process fast
Smooth gently with the back of the comb, a brush or gloved hands
Check with a strand test; rinse within the maker's time, or at once if burning

ul: **Why a short distance from the scalp at first?** Body heat makes the hair near the scalp process faster, and the scalp is the most sensitive area.
**Why the hairline last?** The hair is finer and processes faster.
**Why start the timer when you begin applying?** Processing begins the moment the relaxer touches the hair.
**Never exceed the maker's maximum time.** The recommended time includes application.

blocks.p: A **retouch** relaxes only the **new growth**: the natural hair that has grown from the scalp since the last relaxer. The line where it meets the old relaxed hair is the **line of demarcation**.

flow: Check the record card and the scalp first
Protect the scalp, hairline and ears with base cream as the product needs
Protect the previously relaxed hair with a protective cream or conditioner, as the maker says
Section into four; work in thin partings
Apply the relaxer to the new growth only, stopping at the line of demarcation
Start the timer at the first application
Smooth the new growth gently; do not smooth the relaxer down the old hair
Check the new growth with a strand test; rinse within the time

head: Never overlap
Why
rows: Relaxer on hair that has already been relaxed
It over-processes the hair, which weakens, thins and breaks. The break often happens at the line of demarcation.
Relaxer smoothed down over the old lengths
Same result; smooth only the new growth.

ul: Smooth **gently**, with the back of the comb, a brush or gloved hands. Never pull, and never press hard on the scalp.
Process for **no longer than the maker says**, timed from the start.
Do a strand test during the time: wipe off a little relaxer and see how straight it is; when the hair is straight to the maker's standard, rinse. Do not leave it on 'just to be sure'.
If the client says her scalp is burning, **rinse that area at once with plenty of water**, whatever the time says.

blocks.note: Under-processed hair is still too curly; over-processed hair is weak, limp, gummy and breaks. Under-processing can be fixed later (if the hair is healthy); over-processing cannot.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Rinse **thoroughly with warm water** until no relaxer is left, keeping the hair straight and smoothing it from the roots down.
Direct the water **away from the client's face** so relaxer does not get into her eyes. Protect her ears.
Do not rub or scrub. Use a steady flow.
Keep your gloves on while you rinse.

blocks.p: Rinsing removes the relaxer, but the hair is still very alkaline and swollen. A **neutralising shampoo** stops the chemical action and brings the pH back to normal. Many have a **colour indicator** that changes colour while you lather.

flow: Squeeze out the extra water
Apply the neutralising shampoo and lather gently
Watch the indicator: if it changes colour, relaxer is still in the hair; keep shampooing as the maker says
Rinse well
Repeat as the maker says (often two or three times)
Check the pH or the colour: it should be back to normal

head: After a...
Neutraliser
rows: Hydroxide relaxer (lye or no-lye)
An acid-balanced neutralising shampoo, which stops the action and restores pH. (Not an oxidiser.)
Thio straightener
An oxidising neutraliser (as the maker says), which rebuilds the bonds in the new straight shape.

ul: After neutralising, apply a **conditioner suited to chemically treated hair**, as the maker says. A protein or moisturising treatment may be advised.
Dry and style gently, with **low to medium heat and little tension**. Freshly relaxed hair is weak and swollen.
Do not press or flat iron on the same day. Follow the maker and the instructor.

flow: Throw away any leftover mixed relaxer as the maker says; never save or re-use it
Close and wipe the containers; store them closed and labelled, in a cool, dry place out of reach
Wash and disinfect bowls, brushes and combs
Put towels and capes in the laundry; bin gloves and cotton wool
Wipe spills at once with gloves on; dry the floor
Wash your hands; complete the record card

ul: A **texturiser** loosens the curl pattern but does not straighten the hair. It uses relaxer left on for a shorter time. It is a good choice for a client who wants looser curls with less commitment. Use it as the maker says.
Relaxing is **permanent**: relaxed hair stays straight and will not go back to its natural coils. Only the new growth is natural, so the hair has two textures as it grows out.
A client who wants to go natural can **transition** (grow out the relaxer) or do a **big chop**. The weak spot is the line of demarcation. Advise gentle detangling, moisture and regular trims.
Offer options before a relaxer: a texturiser, a thermal press, braids or twists. Respect her choice.
Natural coily hair is often dry. Check porosity and elasticity before any relaxer, and give treatments first if the hair is weak.

head: Client wants...
Suggest
rows: Straight, smooth hair that lasts for months
A relaxer, if the hair and scalp pass the tests.
Looser curls, not straight
A texturiser, as the maker says.
Straight for a few days or a week
A thermal press (a different unit).
To keep her natural coils but have them easier to manage
Moisture treatments, protective styles, a good routine.
To go natural from relaxed
Transition advice and trims.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, many girls get their first relaxer very young. Be gentle and honest with parents: a relaxer is permanent, the scalp can burn, and young hair often needs a milder choice or a delay.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Problems, first aid, safety and aftercare

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Client's scalp is burning during processing
Rinse the area at once with plenty of water, neutralise, tell the instructor, record it.
Relaxer splashes in the eye

Rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean running water for a long time (as the safety data sheet says, at least 15 minutes), with the eye held open and water running away from the other eye. Do not rub. Get medical help at once.
Chemical burn on the scalp after the service
Rinse with cool water, record it, report it, advise medical help. No grease or home remedies.
Hair breaks or feels gummy during the service
Stop, rinse at once, neutralise gently and condition; report it.
Under-processed hair
Do not re-relax today; reassess and rebook.
Over-processed hair
Neutralise, condition, protein then moisture treatments, trim; no more chemicals until it recovers.
Relaxer on skin
Rinse with plenty of water at once; use the maker's guidance.
Spill
Wipe at once with gloves on; dry the floor.

blocks.note: Report every incident to the instructor and write it in the accident book. Do not re-relax hair or a scalp that has been burnt or has broken until it has recovered and a doctor agrees.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Follow the maker's instructions, the **safety data sheet** and the Centre's rules. Know that these chemicals burn.
Never mix brands, or mix a hydroxide relaxer with a thio product or any other chemical.
Mix a no-lye activator into the cream **just before use**; do not mix more than you need.
Store relaxers **closed and labelled, in a cool, dry place, out of reach** of children and away from heat; check dates.
Throw away leftover **mixed** relaxer as the maker says. Do not pour back or keep it.
Wipe spills with gloves on; dispose of waste as the Centre's rules say.
Clean and disinfect tools after use; launder towels and capes.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Do not scratch the scalp; tell the salon if it is sore
Broken skin can burn or get infected.
Use a gentle shampoo and conditioner; condition regularly
Relaxed hair is weaker and drier.
Low heat with a protectant; no tight styles
Weak hair breaks easily.
Wear a satin scarf or bonnet; protect from sun and sea water
Smooth fabric protects; sun and salt dry the hair.
Wait the time the maker says before colour
Chemicals together over-stress the hair.
Retouch only the new growth, at the interval the stylist advises
Prevents overlap and breakage.

ul: Date, product, strength, base or no-base.
Tests: skin, strand, porosity, elasticity; results.
Scalp condition, new growth in centimetres.
Timing, neutralising and conditioning used.
Result, any problems, advice given and the client's agreement.
I can explain how a hydroxide relaxer breaks disulphide bonds (lanthionisation) and why it is dangerous to skin and eyes.
I can describe lye, no-lye and thio products and a texturiser, and say why thio and hydroxide must never be mixed.
I can choose a mild, regular or super strength from the analysis, strand test and maker's instructions.
I can ask the right questions and check the scalp for abrasions, cuts and sores.
I can do and read skin, strand, porosity, elasticity and incompatibility tests.
I can say when I must not go ahead and rebook instead.
I can put on PPE and protect the client with a cape and base cream.
I can explain why the hair is not shampooed before a hydroxide relaxer.
I can section the dry hair into four and apply base cream for base and no-base relaxers.
I can apply a virgin relaxer in the right order and time it from the first application.
I can do a retouch on new growth only, protect the old hair, and explain why overlap breaks hair.
I can smooth gently, rinse thoroughly, and use a neutralising shampoo with a colour indicator.
I can condition and style freshly relaxed hair gently.
I can deal with a burning scalp, relaxer in the eye, a chemical burn and breakage.
I can store, handle and dispose of relaxers safely, give aftercare, and fill in the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the step and the reason: 'I apply to the new growth only because overlapping over-processes hair that was relaxed before, and it breaks.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A chemical product that permanently straightens or loosens curly hair.
The permanent change of bonds that a hydroxide relaxer makes in the hair.
A relaxer with sodium hydroxide; usually a base relaxer.
A relaxer with guanidine hydroxide, made by mixing a cream with an activator just before use.
A product with ammonium thioglycolate, neutralised with an oxidiser.
A relaxer used for a short time to loosen the curl without straightening.
A protective cream on the scalp, hairline and ears.
Hair that has never been relaxed.
Hair grown from the scalp since the last relaxer.
Where new growth meets relaxed hair; the weakest point.
Putting relaxer on hair that was already relaxed, causing over-processing.
A shampoo that stops the relaxer's action and restores pH.
A scale of acidity and alkalinity; 7 is neutral, below 7 acid, above 7 alkaline.
Hair left too long under a relaxer: weak, limp, gummy and breaking.
Hair still too curly because the relaxer did not work long enough.
The maker's sheet on hazards, storage and first aid.
The client's agreement to the service after the risks are explained.

c1.title: A first relaxer for a schoolgirl in Mandeville
c1.text: Mrs. Sandra Lewis brings her daughter Amoya, 12, to a salon in Mandeville for a first relaxer before the new school year. Amoya's hair is fine and healthy, shoulder-length and natural. She had a few scratches on the scalp from a head-lice comb treatment last week, which are scabbed over. She had her hair washed this morning at home. The trainee, Tanisha, has a regular-strength lye relaxer and a mild no-lye kit.

c2.title: A retouch in Portmore
c2.text: Marcia Johnson, 36, has a retouch booked at a salon in Portmore. Her last relaxer was ten weeks ago, and she has about 3 cm of new growth. She says her hair has been 'breaking at the back' since her last visit, when the stylist 'ran the relaxer through to the ends to even it out'. Trainee Ricardo notices a thin line where the hair is short and weak, about 3 cm from the scalp. The scalp looks healthy.

c3.title: A burning scalp in Falmouth
c3.text: During a practical on a real client in the Centre's salon in Falmouth, trainee Kerry-Ann has applied a relaxer to the new growth of Mrs. Beryl Grant, 41. Seven minutes into a 15-minute process, Mrs. Grant says her scalp is starting to burn at the crown. Kerry-Ann says it is only tingling and tells her to stay still until the timer rings.

c4.title: Hair history in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: Nadine Walker, 28, asks for a relaxer at a salon in Savanna-la-Mar. Her hair has been straightened with a thio product two months ago. She also uses a 'grey cover' lotion from a shop that she cannot name. Her elasticity test shows the hair stretches a long way and does not spring back. Trainee Devon wants to give her a regular relaxer today.

c5.title: Neutralising and clean-up in St. Ann's Bay
c5.text: In the training salon in St. Ann's Bay, trainee Shanice has rinsed a relaxer from a training head and applied a neutralising shampoo. The colour indicator turns pink while she lathers. She is in a hurry and starts to condition. After the session, a bowl of mixed no-lye relaxer remains, and a relaxer jar is left open on a shelf above a sunny window.

questions.q: What should Tanisha do about the scabbed scratches on Amoya's scalp?
o: Put the relaxer on, keeping it a little away from the scabs
Cover the scabs with a thick layer of base cream and go ahead
Not relax today; explain kindly and rebook once it heals
Wash the scalp well first, to clean out the scratches
questions.why: Relaxer on broken skin burns badly. Abrasions mean no relaxer today; explain kindly and rebook when the scalp has fully healed.

questions.q: Amoya's hair was washed this morning. How does this affect the service?
o: Washing may irritate the scalp, so re-check it and follow the maker
It does not matter; hair should always be shampooed before a relaxer
A wash makes it work faster, so the time should be cut by half
A wash means the hair now needs a stronger relaxer to work
questions.why: The scalp's natural oil helps protect it, and washing or rubbing can irritate it. The scalp must be checked again, and the maker's rule followed.

questions.q: For Amoya's fine, healthy hair, which choice is most suitable if the service goes ahead later?
o: A super-strength lye relaxer, to be sure of getting results
A regular lye relaxer, left on for the full maximum time
A thio product mixed in with the hydroxide relaxer to soften it
A mild strength, after a strand test and as the maker says
questions.why: Fine hair processes quickly and needs the mildest effective strength, decided by the analysis, strand test and maker's instructions. Never mix thio and hydroxide products.

questions.q: Mrs. Lewis asks if Amoya's hair will go back to curly if she doesn't like it. What is the true answer?
o: Yes, it will curl back up gradually after the next few washes
No; relaxed hair stays straight, only new growth is natural
Yes, if she rinses it with vinegar after every wash
Yes, within a month, once the relaxer has worn off the hair
questions.why: Relaxers permanently change the bonds. The relaxed hair does not go back; only new growth is natural, so it must be grown out or cut off.

questions.q: Why has Marcia's hair broken at the back?
o: The relaxer was left on for far too short a time
Relaxer went over hair that was already relaxed
Her new growth is too thick for the relaxer to work
She washed her hair too often between visits
questions.why: Overlapping relaxer on hair that is already relaxed over-processes it, so it weakens and breaks, often at the line of demarcation.

questions.q: Where must Ricardo stop applying the relaxer on Marcia's head?
o: At the mid-lengths, so that the whole head blends in evenly
At the ends, once all the new growth has been covered
At the nape, once the back sections have been done
At the line of demarcation, leaving the old hair alone
questions.why: A retouch goes on the new growth only. The older relaxed hair is protected as the maker says, because relaxer on it over-processes it and it breaks.

questions.q: What is the line of demarcation?
o: Where new growth meets relaxed hair, the weakest point
The place on the scalp where the base cream stops going on
The fine hairline at the front of the head
The parting line between two of the four sections
questions.why: It is where the natural hair meets the relaxed hair. The two textures pull against each other, so it is the weak point on the strand.

questions.q: Which action is right for Ricardo's timing?
o: Time from when the last section is finished
Time by feel
Time from the first application and keep within the maker's time
Leave it on until the hair is completely straight, whatever the time
questions.why: Processing begins as soon as the relaxer touches the hair, so the timer starts at the first application and must not pass the maker's time.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do when Mrs. Grant says her scalp is burning?
o: Wait until the timer rings, then rinse as planned
Put more base cream on the burning area and keep going
Smooth the relaxer through faster to finish sooner
Rinse the area at once with plenty of water; report it
questions.why: A burning scalp is a warning. Rinse at once with plenty of water, whatever the time says, and tell the instructor. A burn gets worse the longer the chemical stays on.

questions.q: After rinsing, the scalp shows red, sore areas. What next?
o: Apply a thick layer of oil to soothe the burning skin
Rinse with cool water, record it and advise a doctor
Re-relax the sore area gently once the redness has gone
Tell her it will settle on its own, and keep no record
questions.why: A chemical burn needs rinsing, a record in the accident book, a report to the instructor and medical advice. Oil and grease trap the chemical, and burnt skin must not be relaxed again.

questions.q: What was wrong with Kerry-Ann's reply that it was 'only tingling'?
o: Nothing; some tingling is normal and safe to ignore
She should have told the client it was an allergy
She ignored a warning; burning means rinse at once
She should have used a stronger relaxer on the crown
questions.why: Burning is not normal. By the time redness shows the damage is done, so the client's word is enough to stop and rinse.

questions.q: If relaxer splashed into Mrs. Grant's eye, what should be done?
o: Rinse with plenty of clean running water; get medical help
Rub the eye gently with a clean damp towel to wipe it out
Put a few drops of oil in the eye to soothe and neutralise it
Wait ten minutes to see whether the stinging settles
questions.why: Relaxer is strongly alkaline and can damage the eye quickly. Rinse at once with plenty of clean running water, with the lid held open, and get medical help.

questions.q: What does the thio history mean for Devon's plan to use a regular hydroxide relaxer today?
o: No: thio and hydroxide clash and can break the hair
Yes, if he reduces the processing time by a third
Yes, once the hair has been shampooed to remove the thio
Yes, if he relaxes the new growth only and nothing else
questions.why: Hydroxide on hair with thio treatment can cause severe breakage. Never put one over the other: check the history first.

questions.q: Which test is needed because of the unnamed grey-cover lotion?
o: A pull test on a small bunch of hair, and nothing else
A skin test behind the ear, and nothing else
An incompatibility test on cut hairs, for metallic salts
No test is needed, because lotions from a shop are always mild
questions.why: Grey-cover lotions often contain metallic salts, which react with chemicals and damage hair. The incompatibility test checks for this.

questions.q: Her elasticity test shows the hair stretches a long way and does not spring back. What should Devon advise?
o: Relax today, but with a mild relaxer and a short time
No relaxer now; give treatments first, then retest
Use a stronger relaxer to straighten the weak hair
Colour the hair first to give it body, then relax it
questions.why: Hair that over-stretches and does not return has a weak cortex. Chemicals would break it, so treatments come first.

questions.q: What does the pink indicator mean?
o: The hair is fully neutralised and ready for the conditioner
The shampoo is old, so a fresh bottle should be opened
The hair needs a second light coat of relaxer first
Relaxer is still in the hair; keep shampooing and rinsing
questions.why: A colour-indicator shampoo changes colour while there is still relaxer in the hair. Keep shampooing and rinsing until it stops changing, as the maker says.

questions.q: What is the correct way to deal with the leftover mixed no-lye relaxer?
o: Pour it back into the jar
Throw it away as the maker says
Keep it for tomorrow
Add water and use it on another head
questions.why: Mixed relaxer begins to work and loses strength, and it must never be saved or put back. Dispose of it as the maker and the Centre's rules say.

questions.q: What is wrong with the open relaxer jar on the shelf above the sunny window?
o: It should be closed, labelled and kept cool and dry
Nothing is wrong, since relaxer keeps well in any light
It should be moved to a lower shelf near the basin
It should be mixed with water so that it does not dry out
questions.why: Relaxers must be stored closed and labelled in a cool, dry place out of reach. Heat and air spoil them and an open jar is a hazard.

questions.q: After a thio straightener has softened the bonds, what does the oxidising neutraliser do?
o: Lifts the cuticle so conditioner can enter
Washes out the base cream from the scalp
Makes the hair more alkaline for a second pass
Rebuilds the bonds in the new straight shape
questions.why: Thio products break bonds by reduction; an oxidising neutraliser reverses this and fixes the hair in its straight shape. It is not used after a hydroxide relaxer, which needs an acid-balanced neutralising shampoo.

questions.q: A client with 4 cm of new growth asks the trainee to relax her whole head 'to even it out'. What should the trainee explain?
o: The whole head, as long as a mild strength is used on it
The ends as well, provided they are done last and quickly
Only the new growth; going over old hair breaks it
The old hair too, provided base cream is put on it first
questions.why: Overlapping relaxer onto hair that is already relaxed over-processes it. The old hair is left alone, and the client is told that regular trims even up the ends instead.
